title: Phoenix: Learning Scene Structure Representations for Generalizable World-Action Models
authors: Yupeng Zheng; Chaoyue Li; Linbo Wang; Xiang Li; Yuhang Zheng; Xiaotong Su; Songen Gu; Yichen Zhang; Zebin Xing; Shuai Tian; Jingxiang Guo; Jing Li; Zhiyong Zhao; Zhongpu Xia; Qichao Zhang; Haoran Li; Shuicheng Yan; Dongbin Zhao
abstract: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet reconstruction-oriented visual representations do not explicitly emphasize the spatial relationships and object-state changes needed for manipulation. We introduce Phoenix, which learns representations of scene structure for world-action modeling. Specifically, Phoenix Encoder enriches DINOv3's general visual semantics through dual-teacher distillation of geometric and spatiotemporal semantic knowledge. Next, CS-VAE causally aggregates and compresses Phoenix Encoder features into generative latents while preserving scene information and spatial layout. Finally, Phoenix jointly predicts these latents, complementary appearance latents, and robot actions, linking scene evolution with action generation. To study pretraining data efficiency, we curate approximately 39,000 hours of egocentric and robot manipulation data for representation learning and use the robot demonstration subset for WAM pretraining. Following benchmark-specific post-training, Phoenix achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-robot benchmarks spanning single-arm, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation. It demonstrates strong robustness to perturbations, achieving success rates of 94.8% on LIBERO-Plus and 72.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 C2R, alongside strong cross-embodiment transfer and real-world manipulation performance on Bench2Dex and RoboDojo-RealWorld, respectively. Pretraining-scale analysis shows larger performance gains from data scaling than a video-VAE-only baseline, indicating stronger scaling benefits and more effective data utilization. Moreover, Phoenix maintains high success rates when adapted with limited downstream demonstrations, demonstrating strong few-shot adaptation. Our code, pretraining data, and models are available on the project page to help the community reproduce our results.

title: A Principled Approach to Concurrency, Nondeterminism, and Asynchrony in Choreographies
authors: Xueying Qin; Marco Peressotti; Fabrizio Montesi
abstract: Choreographic programming (CP) describes a distributed system as a global program and compiles it into communicating network programs via endpoint projection (EPP). Asynchrony captures the independent progress of communicating processes, while nondeterminism captures the range of behaviours that can arise from their interactions. However, the integration of both features into a theory of CP is absent. We present Nyarlathotep, the first asynchronous nondeterministic CP framework. We define its operational semantics of choreographies and networks using labelled transition systems. Besides asynchrony and choreographic nondeterminism, Nyarlathotep supports expressive features including general branching, out-of-order execution, and general recursion with parameterised procedures that processes can enter independently. We prove EPP sound and complete, establishing strong behavioural equivalence between the semantics of choreographies and their projected networks. We prove that projected networks are communication-safe and deadlock-free. We mechanised all our results in Lean 4.

title: SIRAZ: Sparse Inter-Layer Residual Aggregation for Zero-Shot Visual Neural Decoding
authors: Neha; Mudasir Ganaie
abstract: Brain-computer interfaces aim to establish direct communication between neural activity and external systems, making interpretation of brain signals an important problem. In this context, neural visual decoding seeks to infer visual information from neural activity by learning a mapping between brain responses and the corresponding visual stimuli. It investigates how visual information emerges from neural signals and relates to perceptual processing while enabling the reconstruction or retrieval of visual stimuli from neural signals. Our brain primarily follows a hierarchical pathway to process visual information captured by the eye. However, neural representations learned by existing methods differ fundamentally from those produced by the biological visual system. To bridge this gap and mimic the human vision hierarchy, we introduce Sparse Inter-layer Residual Aggregation for Zero-shot (SIRAZ). SIRAZ is a framework that aligns neural visual representations by jointly modeling early visual processes via fovea- and magnocellular-pathway-inspired Difference-of-Gaussians transformations. To align the semantic information with neural information, it extracts multiple intermediate representations of the image at multiple depths and passes them through the Residual Gated Adapter Mechanism. To study the temporal dynamics of neural signals, the Direction-aware Multi-Scale Temporal Attention Encoder is introduced to align the learned neural representation with the final visual representation. The proposed framework achieves 92.5% top-1 and 99.27% top-5 accuracy in the intra-subject setting on the THINGS-EEG dataset, and 50.25% and 75% top-1 and top-5 accuracy in the THINGS-MEG dataset. The results indicate that combining biologically motivated visual representations with the structured modalities of neural dynamics improves cross-modal alignment and zero-shot image retrieval.

title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
authors: Langtian Qin; Avishkar Dnyaneshwar Kawadgave; Ian Andrew Harshbarger; Leïla Nasraoui; Carla Fabiana Chiasserini; Marco Levorato
abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.

title: Physical Layer Security for Digital Semantic Communication: A Bit-Level Perspective
authors: Seonjung Kim; Jaehyeok Kim; Yo-Seb Jeon
abstract: Digital semantic communication requires reliable recovery of task-relevant information at a legitimate receiver while limiting source reconstruction by an eavesdropper. Uniform bit protection, however, does not account for the heterogeneous reliability and secrecy requirements of semantic bits. This paper proposes a bit-level physical layer security (PLS) framework that learns these requirements and incorporates them into physical-layer resource allocation. We first introduce a wiretap semantic feature channel whose two-stage training learns per-bit target bit-flip probabilities for the legitimate receiver (Bob) and the eavesdropper (Eve). These targets characterize the reliability requirements at Bob and the secrecy protection requirements against Eve. Based on the learned targets, we formulate a joint power and artificial-noise (AN) allocation problem for a multiple-input single-output wiretap channel under a worst-case angular-separation model. For a given target profile, the optimal information-AN power split admits a closed-form solution, and the per-bit power allocation is obtained by water-filling. We further develop a leakage-aware selection method among multiple learned-target profiles and extend the design to multiple-input multiple-output channels. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a better trade-off between preserving reconstruction quality at Bob and degrading that at Eve than uniform power allocation and the evaluated learning-based secure semantic communication schemes.

title: Drift-Aware Adaptive Semantic Codec Update Strategy for Dynamic Semantic Communications
authors: Bizhu Wang; Manqi Li; Shujun Han; Mengying Sun; Xiaodong Xu
abstract: Semantic communication reduces transmission overhead by conveying task-relevant semantic features, but its performance depends on the consistency between training and target-domain data distributions. In dynamic environments, distribution drift can make offline-trained semantic codec models stale and degrade transmission performance. Frequent updates alleviate this degradation but increase communication, computation, and queueing costs, whereas infrequent updates delay model adaptation. To address this tradeoff, we propose a drift-aware adaptive update strategy for dynamic semantic communication systems. Drift intensity is quantified in the semantic feature space, and Drift-Aware Age of Model (DA-AoM) is introduced to jointly capture drift-induced performance degradation, drift-dependent update service delay, and conventional update latency. Closed-form average DA-AoM expressions are derived for edge-layer M/M/1 and cloud-layer D/M/1 update scenarios, based on which the update frequency is optimized under the queueing-stability constraint. Simulations show that DA-AoM captures the joint effects of drift intensity, computing rate, bandwidth, and update frequency on model freshness beyond conventional Age of Information (AoI). The proposed strategy reduces average DA-AoM by 9.2\%--42.4\% compared with representative baselines under the same resource constraints.

title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
authors: Giovanni Adorni; Daniele Grosso
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

title: DAQ: Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Transformers
authors: Jialin Chen; Xiaochen Zhao; Aili Wang
abstract: Spiking transformers combine attention-based representation learning with sparse spike communication, yet their weights and membrane variables still incur substantial storage and computation overhead. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a practical way to reduce these overheads, but preserving neuronal firing under weight and membrane quantization remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Decision-Aligned Post-Training Quantization (DAQ), a method that calibrates the quantizers to align neuronal firing decisions with those of a floating-point reference. We analyze how errors from these quantizers affect firing at decision boundaries and how they propagate over time steps in recurrent neurons. Based on this analysis, we formulate an objective that encourages quantized membrane variables to remain within the reference firing regions along the quantized model's own state trajectory. Experiments across multiple spiking transformer architectures on image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking demonstrate the effectiveness of DAQ with 4-bit weights and membrane variables. On FE108, DAQ achieves 58.8\% AUC and 90.9\% PR with SDTrack, while reducing energy by 66.2\%.

title: Active Contrast-Dissipation All-Optical Encryption
authors: Dongyang Du; Zixuan Fu; Fei Dai; Hang Chen
abstract: Optical encryption is meant to place secrecy in physical structure, yet adversaries can readily construct imperfect physical keys to probe the encryption system via trial-and-error iterations. Such systems inevitably leak target plaintext information and preserve invertible residual structural features, rendering the entire encryption scheme vulnerable to adversarial inversion attacks. Here, we report an active contrast-dissipation all-optical encryption architecture, which partitions wavefront modulation into M wavelength-private encryption layers and N shared decoding layers. Security rests on multi-dimensional physical keys that must match simultaneously, including illumination wavelength, precise spatial alignment and layer stacking sequence. With every key matched and authorized readout is preserved: the composite plaintext is reconstructed at a full-detector Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) of 0.997. We further impose active contrast dissipation as a core security constraint. Under physical perturbation it suppresses the foreground-background intensity contrast, so that the slightest key mismatch collapses the target features and dissipates the plaintext into randomized, diffuse speckle within chaotic background noise, leaving no residual semantic leakage to invert. Under nanoscale wavelength detuning, a 1 degree in-plane rotation, a single-pixel lateral displacement or layer-stacking tampering, the plaintext vanishes and the PCC approaches zero, whereas conventional diffractive encryptors retain identifiable contours. This work provide a feasible and reliable solution for high-security information encryption, with great application potential in communication security, information anti-counterfeiting, and confidential data storage.

title: Semantic Communication via Analog RF Computing: When the Radio Computes the Meaning
authors: Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas
abstract: Semantic communication (SC) systems transmit continuous latent representations of meaning, but computing the semantic encoder at resource-constrained edge devices incurs substantial energy and memory costs. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end SC framework that executes the semantic encoder in the client's RF receiver front end using analog RF computing. A base station (BS) broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, while each edge device reuses its receiver's passive mixer to compute semantic latents at ultra-low energy. These latents are transmitted over the uplink for network-side task inference. We show that analog computing noise across encoder layers and channel noise affecting transmitted latents admit a unified mathematical model. We define a task-posterior semantic distortion metric and derive its second-order decomposition into per-client, per-stage semantic sensitivities. Using this decomposition, we obtain a closed-form semantic-aware water-filling allocation of the total client energy budget across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks, assigning tighter accuracy targets to semantically sensitive stages. This allocation induces a broadcast beamforming problem that accounts for client-specific, per-layer accuracy requirements. We further refine the allocation through stochastic optimization and jointly design it with multi-task noise-aware training of the shared semantic model. MNIST simulations show that, at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2\%-19.2\% compared with uniform precision and 5.1\%-13.1\% compared with client-blind allocation. Noise-aware co-design yields a further 46\% reduction.

title: DYNAMICS OF PORTFOLIO ASSESSMENT STRATEGY IN EVALUATING THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE SKILLS FOR PUPILS WITH HEARING IMPAIRMENTS IN FAKO DIVISION, SOUTH WEST REGION OF CAMEROON
authors: Ngenwie Emilia Tanyie; Therese Mungah Shalo Tchombe
venue: International Journal of Developmental Issues in Education and Humanities
abstract: This study examined the impact of portfolio assessment on evaluating the English language skills of pupils with hearing impairment in Fako Division, Cameroon. Portfolio assessment, as an informal and learner-centred approach, was explored within the framework of inclusive education, where traditional assessment methods often fail to adequately reflect the abilities of learners with hearing loss. The research utilised a quasi-experimental design involving pupils with hearing impairment in selected inclusive primary schools. Data were gathered through English language tests, classroom observations, and interviews with parents, teachers, head teachers, and the divisional delegate. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, and regression analysis, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. The results indicated that pupils subjected to portfolio assessment performed significantly better in English language skills than those assessed through conventional methods. Statistical analysis (SPSS t-tests and regression) showed that pupils assessed via portfolios scored notably higher on post-tests (portfolio group mean=12.78 versus control=11.14; t(38)=2.919, p<.05). Regression analysis demonstrated that portfolio use was a strong predictor of language improvement (β=0.336, p<.001). Classroom observations and interview findings further revealed that portfolio assessment encouraged ongoing learning, increased learner engagement, self-reflection, and heightened teacher awareness of individual progress. The study concludes that portfolio assessment is an effective method for evaluating the English language skills of pupils with hearing impairment and recommends its systematic adoption within inclusive classroom practice.

title: From Embedded Finance to Embedded Obligation: A Law-and-Economics Theory of Consumer Protection in Platform-Mediated Financial Services
authors: Yongxin Chen
abstract: Embedded finance is usually described as the integration of financial services into non-financial platforms. This article argues that the deeper regulatory transformation is the embedding of future legal and economic obligations into ordinary consumption, work, business, and entertainment environments. When credit, payment, wage-advance, wallet, and merchant-financing functions are delivered through plat form architecture, consumer protection cannot focus only on the formal product or licensed provider. It must also examine how obligations are framed, made salient or obscure, personalized through data, and allocated across platforms, merchants, lenders, and technical intermediaries. The article develops a law and-economics theory of Embedded Obligation Architecture, explains its irreducible object, refines its four layers, and distinguishes it from choice architecture, digital nudging, dark patterns, behavioral contract theory, and platform governance. It specifies the evidentiary limits of transferring behavioral evidence to embedded-finance contexts and proposes a Functional Embedded Obligation Test as a standard with gateway elements, evidentiary thresholds, legal vehicles, safe harbors, and proportionate remedies.

title: The Sociolinguistics of Machine Identity: LLM Personality and Ideology Propagation
authors: Guangni Li
abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) possess a measurable "personality," and how do the linguistic properties of training corpora shape their cognitive style and downstream reasoning? This paper approaches these questions from a sociolinguistic perspective on machine "identity." This manuscript is positioned explicitly as a conceptual perspective paper: it does not present original experimental data, nor does it constitute a systematic review with defined search strategies or inclusion criteria. Instead, it synthesises key published findings into two original theoretical frameworks intended to guide future empirical and engineering work. We examine evidence that LLMs exhibit reliable, valid Big Five personality traits—particularly in large, instruction-tuned models—and that continued pre-training on domain-specific corpora may shape those traits through measurable linguistic features: imperative ratio, type-token ratio (TTR), and syntactic complexity. We then analyse how standard-language ideology embedded in training corpora is amplified in model outputs, disadvantaging dialect and minority-language communities. Building on these findings, we propose two conceptual contributions: (1) a Personality Engineering (PE) framework for targeted continued pre-training to cultivate task-appropriate cognitive profiles, and (2) a Language Ideology Propagation Model (LIPM) mapping the pipeline from corpus composition to societal impact. Both frameworks are explicitly conceptual and require empirical validation before they can function as operational guidelines. Their value lies in structuring future research and providing a shared vocabulary for cross-disciplinary collaboration, with direct implications for responsible AI deployment.

title: From Legal Databases to AI-Assisted Justice: A Risk-Sensitive Framework for the Application of Information Technologies in Law
authors: Li Yongxin
abstract: This paper analyzes information technologies in law and proposes a risk-sensitive framework for responsible digital legal practice. Using EU regulatory developments as the main legal lens, while also referring to international standards and policy materials, the study reviews legal databases, case-management systems, artificial intelligence and natural language processing, electronic identification and signatures, digital evidence, online dispute resolution and electronic courts. The paper's contribution is to connect general principles of transparency, human oversight, source verification and accountability to concrete stages of legal work: intake, research, drafting, identity assurance, signing, archiving and audit. Brief examples of AI-assisted drafting, online dispute resolution and electronic signature verification illustrate the practical use of the framework. The analysis concludes that digital legal systems create value when they remain traceable, proportionate and subject to professional responsibility rather than replacing legal judgment.

title: Measuring Activity-Space Segregation with Multi-Source Big Data: A Physical--Digital Framework with Simulation Validation and a Real-Data Proof of Concept
authors: Guangwei Wang
abstract: Segregation research increasingly measures who people encounter beyond home, yet physical mobility, place semantics, and digital activity are often combined without clear construct boundaries. This study develops a physical--digital activity-space framework that distinguishes co-presence, digital exposure, and digital interaction, and represents physical and digital segregation as separate components rather than a forced composite. Validation is deliberately split by evidentiary role. A public Washington--Baltimore Foursquare check-in subset tests the computational feasibility and robustness of a discrete group co-visitation statistic; it does not validate continuous socioeconomic exposure because the dataset lacks individual socioeconomic status. Monte Carlo experiments separately test layer-selective construct response and sensitivity to trace missingness, spatial aggregation, socioeconomic measurement error, and cross-layer coupling. The results show that the proposed calculations are executable and that the synthetic physical and digital components respond selectively to their generating mechanisms, while also revealing important measurement attenuation. No real-data estimate of income segregation, digital exposure, physical--digital coupling, or the causal effect of inequality is reported. The framework therefore combines bounded validation with a falsifiable comparative and causal research agenda.

title: From Chopin to Kitsch? Pauline Viardot's Vocal Mazurkas and the popularisation of classical music
authors: Stacy Olive Jarvis
venue: Journal of Music Theory and Transcultural Music Studies
abstract: This article examines the concept of ‘popular music’ in the context of the work of Frédéric Chopin (1810–1849). The paper analyses six mazurkas by the Polish composer and their transcription for voice and piano, performed by the opera diva Pauline Viardot (1821–1910) to words by the French poet Louis Pomme (1831–1901). This chamber vocal cycle, composed by Viardot, illustrates the established poetics of the salons of the second third of the 19th century, where literature and music converged. Based on an analysis of various sources, this study examines the history of the works’ creation, their imagery and intonation, as well as the harmonic features of these vocal miniatures, whilst reconstructing their context. As a result, a connection is revealed between Viardot’s vocal mazurkas and Chopin’s songs, composed between 1829 and 1847, in the themes of love and loneliness. The aim of this article is to investigate how the opera singer bridges the gap between classical music and the mass audience and becomes a creator of kitsch. The research methodology includes an analysis of historical sources, as well as a musical and literary analysis of Chopin’s and Viardot’s mazurkas. The author concludes that kitsch emerges at the intersection of classical and popular music, where the integration of various elements from different mazurkas helps Viardot achieve a precise correspondence between the expressive content of the text and Chopin’s musical language.

title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
authors: Hanna David
venue: Journal of Child Development, Exceptionality and Education
abstract: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent games and serious real-world aggression remains more contested, with recent research emphasizing relatively small effects and the importance of individual and contextual factors. Overall, the evidence suggests that the developmental consequences of gaming for children and adolescents depend less on gaming itself than on the duration, content, context, and pattern of engagement.

title: Enmification and De/Reconstruction of the Self at Guantánamo: U.S. Political-Legal Discourse and Mansoor Adayfi's Life Narrative
authors: Olga Kajtár-Pinjung
venue: SZTE Repository of Dissertations (University of Szeged)
abstract: Guantánamo Bay has been a symbol of alleged human rights violations and indefinite detention for over two decades.Located on the island of Cuba, the naval base has been operated by the United States since 1903, and following the 9/11 terrorist attacks, it was designated to be a detention facility for the suspected terrorists captured in the War on Terror.The present doctoral dissertation examines two types of image construction related to Guantánamo: constructing the image of the enemy and constructing the image of the self.The dissertation explores the discrepancies and overlaps between the macro-narrative constructed by the U.S. government between 2001 and 2024 and the micro-narrative of former detainee Mansoor Adayfi.Through the analysis of presidential rhetoric and legislative measures, the dissertation investigates the deliberate processes of enemy-image construction (enmification) of Guantánamo detainees by the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Joseph R.Biden, and Donald J. Trump.In parallel, it examines the systematic deconstruction of Adayfi's sense of self through practices of mortification and enhanced interrogation, as well as the subsequent reconstruction of the self through building a community, resisting, finding purpose, and using humor, thus rebuilding his self with efforts to counter the enemy image, as presented in Adayfi's memoir.The dissertation analyzes the clash between the legally imposed and enforced enemy subject position and the subject positions articulated in Adayfi's life narrative.By juxtaposing the macro-level political discourse and legislative enmification with a personal life narrative, the research exposes inconsistencies and the purposeful construction of an enemy image that the personal account challenges.The research emphasizes the significance of an interdisciplinary approach, illustrating how the comparative analysis of legal and literary sources enables a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the emification of Guantánamo detainees and the de/reconstruction of the self.First and foremost, I would like to express my deepest gratitude to my supervisors, Dr. habil Ágnes Zsófia Kovács and Dr. habil.Zoltán Vajda, for their continued support and invaluable help not only in the last four years but during my BA and MA studies as well.Their guidance and trust were imperative, as they allowed me the freedom to follow my instincts and interests while nudging me in the right direction when necessary.

title: Exploration of Connections Between Student Choice of Knowledge Pieces in Solving a Slope Problem and Situational Factors
authors: Kent R. Hoffman
abstract: Even when students have learned the same concept, they often cannot apply it in different situations. This study explored why high school students (ages 13-16) have such difficulty connecting what they learn in math class to science class, and to everyday life. Students were given the same slope problems in different settings: two different math classes and a science class. These problems were chosen to have similar levels of difficulty, with the differences between them being their placement in a science-type problem, a mathematical-type problem, and a real-world scenario. Researchers asked students to explain their thinking through writing or in clinical interviews. The results were eye-opening: when students encountered a problem, the context mattered. If a problem appeared in a math classroom, students would approach it one way, using practices associated with a constant conception and a procedural emphasis. The exact same problem occurred in a science classroom? They’d tackle it completely differently. Most surprisingly, students labeled almost everything as a “math problem” when they were in a math classroom, even when the problem was clearly scientific or real-world. During the clinical interviews, much more was revealed, with students looking for familiarity over perhaps the correct procedures. Students would go to great lengths to justify how they identified a problem, relating it to past experiences. What matters is the label students put on a problem: “this is math” versus “this is science,” which determined which knowledge they used and how they solved it. The classroom setting offered invisible guardrails, channeling students toward certain approaches and preventing them from using knowledge they already had. The study suggests that what prevents students from connecting their learning across disciplines/ subjects is not a lack of knowledge; it is that different classroom environments train them to see problems in fundamentally different ways.

title: Exploring Micronutrient Intake, Ultra-Processed Food Consumption, and Their Associations With Metabolic Syndrome and Food-Related Behaviors Among Adolescents in the United States
authors: Oluyemisi Akinsola
abstract: Adolescence is a period of rapid growth and development during which good nutrition is especially important for long-term health. However, many adolescents in the United States consume large amounts of ultra-processed foods, including packaged snacks, sugary drinks, and fast food. This dissertation used nationally representative data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2017–2020 to examine micronutrient intake, ultra-processed food consumption, food-related behaviors, and metabolic health among U.S. adolescents. The first part of the study examined usual nutrient intake and micronutrient adequacy. Overall micronutrient adequacy was high at 96%. However, important dietary concerns remained. Many adolescents had low intakes of calcium and magnesium and consumed high amounts of saturated fat, added sugars, and sodium. Adolescents who used dietary supplements had higher intakes of several vitamins and minerals, but supplement use did not eliminate all nutrient shortfalls. Ultra-processed foods contributed about two-thirds of total daily energy intake, with differences observed across demographic groups. The second part examined whether food-related behaviors were associated with ultra-processed food consumption and micronutrient adequacy. More frequent fast-food consumption was associated with a higher estimated share of energy from ultra-processed foods, although this relationship was not statistically conclusive. More frequent snacking was associated with slightly higher overall micronutrient adequacy. However, the study did not assess the nutritional quality of individual snacks, so this finding should not be interpreted to mean that more frequent snacking is necessarily healthier. Other behaviors, including nutrition label use, calorie information use, and food-place exposure, showed limited or inconsistent associations with dietary outcomes. The final part examined whether ultra-processed food consumption and micronutrient adequacy helped explain relationships between food-related behaviors and metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risk factors associated with future diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Metabolic syndrome affected about 7% of adolescents in the analytic sample. Neither ultra-processed food consumption nor overall micronutrient adequacy was clearly associated with metabolic syndrome, and the statistical models did not identify significant indirect pathways linking the food-related behaviors examined with metabolic syndrome through these dietary measures. Overall, the findings show that adolescent diet quality is multidimensional. High overall micronutrient adequacy can coexist with high consumption of ultra-processed foods and other unfavorable dietary characteristics. Strategies to improve adolescent nutrition should therefore extend beyond addressing individual nutrient shortfalls and promote dietary patterns that increase nutrient-dense foods while reducing excessive intake of ultra-processed foods, added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium. Nutrition interventions should also consider the specific foods adolescents consume during common eating behaviors, such as snacking and fast-food consumption, rather than focusing only on how frequently these behaviors occur. Future research should examine specific types of ultra-processed foods and snacks and use longitudinal studies to better understand how adolescent dietary patterns and food-related behaviors influence metabolic health over time.

title: The RAIL Principles for Neurosymbolic AI: Reasoning, Assurances, Interfacing and Learning
authors: Artur d’Avila Garcez
abstract: Neurosymbolic AI systems that integrate machine learning and symbolic reasoning are rapidly gaining attention. They complement the data-intensive statistical approaches of neural networks and language models with symbolic reasoning formalism and algorithms to function in high-stakes domains or in low-data regimes that characterize many real-world applications. We argue that the neurosymbolic combination of machine learning and formal reasoning is not a niche approach within AI, but rather includes many already successful techniques that are of crucial importance to the development of reliable, efficient and, ultimately, trustworthy systems. This perspective prompts a re-examination of the design of current AI systems. We show that many leading AI systems can be analysed from the perspective of four principles of neurosymbolic AI design: Reasoning, Assurances, Interfacing and Learning (RAIL). Applying the RAIL framework offers a unified view of seemingly disparate AI systems, ranging from physics-aware machine learning to DeepMind’s Alpha-* suite, causal learning and tool-augmented Large Language Models. Importantly, using the neurosymbolic RAIL principles as a much-needed new evaluation standard for AI will enable engineers to make better-informed and more principled decisions about the design and deployment of production-level AI systems. In this article, we introduce the RAIL principles, examine how they can be applied across major areas of AI, and illustrate how they may guide practitioners to integrate neurosymbolic methods into next-generation AI technologies.
keywords: semantic communications; semantic encoding; semantic channel coding

title: Auditing Representation-Space Fraud Detection: A Bayesian IRL Framework for Calibrated Uncertainty and Its Limits
authors: Shivam Swarup; Divya Prakash Shrivastava; Rakesh Thakur
abstract: Shilling detectors for recommender systems are almost always evaluated by one number, detection AUROC, with no account of when it can be trusted. We audit representation-space detection with VEIL (Variational Evaluation via Inverse-reinforcement Learning), a pairwise (Bradley–Terry) Bayesian reward-inference framework over frozen encoder embeddings, after the Bayesian auditing paradigm for LLM alignment [1]: (A) a base posterior; (B) a hierarchical ARD extension with a learned confidence; and (C) a label-routed organic/attacker mixture used as an evidence-accumulation check. We prove (Prop. 1) that no detector built on a representation invariant to some transformation of user profiles can beat chance against an attack indistinguishable from organic profiles under that invariance. Detection is near-perfect against synthetic-structure attacks (AUROC 0.936–1.000) but collapses under donor-mimicry, which clones a real user’s item set and splices in 1–3 target items: to chance on MovieLens-1M (0.48–0.51), partially on Amazon Musical Instruments, and least on CiaoDVD. Donor-mimicry is not undetectable: a non-learned baseline, each profile’s maximum raw item-set Jaccard similarity to any other, reaches AUROC 0.92–0.97 (average precision 0.50–0.57) on all four donor-mimicry configurations, including ML-1M, where every embedding-based score is at chance. The signal is in the raw profiles; LightGCN’s representation discards it, placing injected profiles closer to their true donor than its zero-propagation MF reduction does (distance 1.98 vs. 3.09). Severity varies by dataset, encoder, and detection method, with no one axis predicting the others. The limit lies in the representation, not the attack, and raw-similarity checks are a necessary complement to any learned detector

title: Recent Advances in Medical Imaging Segmentation: Generative, Few-Shot, Foundation and Universal Models
authors: Fares Bougourzi; Abdenour Hadid
abstract: Medical imaging is a cornerstone of modern healthcare, driving advancements in diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient care. Among its various tasks, segmentation remains one of the most challenging problems due to factors such as data accessibility, annotation complexity, structural variability, variation in medical imaging modalities, and privacy constraints. Despite recent progress, achieving robust generalization and domain adaptation remains a significant hurdle, particularly given the resource-intensive nature of some proposed models and their reliance on domain expertise. This survey explores cutting-edge advancements in medical image segmentation, focusing on methodologies such as Generative AI, Few-Shot Learning, Foundation Models, and Universal Models. These approaches offer promising solutions to longstanding challenges. We provide a comprehensive overview of the theoretical foundations, state-of-the-art techniques, and recent applications of these methods. Finally, we discuss inherent limitations, unresolved issues, and future research directions aimed at enhancing the practicality and accessibility of segmentation models in medical imaging. We maintain a GitHub Repository to continue tracking and updating innovations in this field.

title: Over-the-Air Semantic Alignment via Dual Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces
authors: Mario Edoardo Pandolfo; Kyriakos Stylianopoulos; George C. Alexandropoulos; Paolo Di Lorenzo
abstract: Semantic communications enable task-oriented information exchange, but suffer from latent-space mismatch when transmitter and receiver employ heterogeneous machine learning models. Existing semantic alignment methods rely on digital processing, introducing computational and latency overhead. This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment entirely in the wave domain. By jointly exploiting programmable metasurfaces at both ends of a link and the wireless channel, the proposed architecture realizes an end-to-end linear transformation between heterogeneous latent spaces. We show phase-only multilayer SIM can approximate both supervised linear aligners and zero-shot Parseval-frame equalizers. We investigate single-SIM, disjoint asymmetric and symmetric dual-SIM, and jointly optimized dual-SIM configurations, considering channel equalization and constructive channel exploitation. For joint design, we develop an alternating projected gradient algorithm with convergence guarantees to first-order stationary points. We further introduce a deep-unrolled network that unrolls gradient-based iterations to reduce computational cost of SIM reconfiguration under channel variations. Numerical results with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment from moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios. The joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM designs achieve the highest accuracy over compact channels, the joint design leads at shallow stack depths, and the advantage over single-SIM designs diminishes at equal depth.

title: When the Mythical Man-Month Meets Agentic Web Systems: Structured Coordination for Scalable Development
authors: Zhiyao Wu; Zi Liang; Haibo Hu
abstract: As agentic systems are increasingly deployed to support complex Web tasks, multi-agent architectures offer greater parallelism, specialization, and task coverage. However, increasing the number of agents does not necessarily improve system performance, as communication, synchronization, redundant work, and coordination overhead may offset the benefits of additional agents. This presents a fundamental scaling challenge for agentic Web systems: how can agent populations be organized to balance task performance and coordination costs? To address this challenge, we systematically investigate the relationship between agent population size, per-agent token consumption, and coordination overhead in collaborative agentic systems. Experiments on complex Web-oriented software development tasks reveal a non-linear scaling pattern: per-agent token consumption initially decreases as the agent population grows, but eventually exhibits diminishing returns. Motivated by these findings, we introduce the Surgical Team Model (STM), a structured coordination framework that organizes agents through role specialization, constrained inter-agent communication, and coordinator-mediated task aggregation. Experiments on full-stack Web application development tasks show that STM achieves competitive task completion quality and comparable token consumption relative to representative baselines, while incurring higher execution latency.

title: When Cause Attribution Is Not Enough: Action-Value Control for Task-Oriented Semantic Communication with Discrete Encoder Switching
authors: Moirangthem Tiken Singh
abstract: A task-oriented semantic communication receiver that selects among independently trained encoders must answer two questions when performance degrades: which component is responsible, and which available action best restores task performance. These are distinct decision problems. Under discrete encoder switching, correctly identifying the dominant information-loss component does not necessarily identify the action that most reduces task error. Diagnosis and intervention should therefore be treated as separate problems. We support this finding with two complementary instruments. The first is a receiver-side diagnostic that partitions task-information loss into encoder and channel components and supplies population-valid task-error bounds conditional on one-sided information estimators. The second is an offline-supervised, online label-free action-value controller built from two monotone (isotonic) maps that target a reduction in measured error. The main experiments focus on two complementary axis-aligned actions that cleanly isolate the effect of discrete switching; a pilot further examines a combined action. Evaluation covers a controlled model with closed-form ground truth, three DeepJSCC vision systems, and a non-vision pilot. On STL-10, the diagnosis correctly identifies the larger loss component at 80% of operating points, yet matches the oracle-best action only 25% of the time. Structural mismatch caps any diagnosis-driven loss-ordering policy at 46% accuracy, even with perfect knowledge of the ordering. The action-value controller, which exploits the magnitude of each loss deficit, achieves 0.86, compared to 0.28 for the raw rule. Where the encoder is rarely the bottleneck, the controller naturally retains the physical-layer default, yielding robust and selective intervention.

title: CommJEPA: When Predictive Representation Learning Meets Wireless Intelligence
authors: Feiran You; Hongyang Du; Kang Wei; Jun Li; Abbas Jamalipour
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an integral part of wireless systems, yet much of today's wireless AI remains task-specific and reactive, with models typically trained to map current observations to predefined outputs or reconstruct observed data. While effective for individual tasks, such approaches provide limited support for learning what is predictable, reusable, and transferable in dynamic wireless environments. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) offers a different perspective by learning predictive representations in latent space that capture informative structure in the observations. In this article, we introduce Communication JEPA (CommJEPA) as a communication-oriented framework for predictive representation learning. The central idea is bidirectional. JEPA can equip wireless systems with predictive representations for capturing latent channel and environmental dynamics, integrating heterogeneous observations, adapting to changing conditions, and supporting future decisions. Conversely, the physical structure, partial observability, multiple time scales, action-dependent evolution, and resource constraints of wireless systems motivate new communication-aware JEPA designs. We develop this mutual perspective, organize the resulting design space, and discuss representative JEPA-based wireless instantiations for prediction and control. We further highlight open challenges toward scalable, interactive, and predictive wireless intelligence.

title: Be My Eye: Learning to See Beyond a Robot's Own Perspective
authors: Baifu Huang; Shilin Fang; Jianan Wang
abstract: Robots operating in the real world are inherently subject to partial observability, particularly in multi-robot collaboration, where individual observations may be insufficient for effective task execution. A key challenge is leveraging complementary observations from partner robots to support collaborative decision-making. We argue that information sharing should go beyond passively transmitting raw observations or generic visual features. Instead, robots should selectively encode task-relevant information according to task objectives and execution progress. To this end, we propose a task-oriented active context sharing framework that transforms robot observations into compact representations, preserving critical information under constrained communication budgets. The framework adopts a two-stage training paradigm. In the first stage, onboard observations and task instructions are jointly encoded into compact context representations. Task-oriented future prediction and soft task-progress correspondence learning guide this collaboration-agnostic compression, preserving information about task objectives and execution progress. In the second stage, the learned representations are integrated into a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy, enabling bidirectional context exchange. Each robot combines complementary partner information with local observations to guide action generation. Action supervision jointly refines the context representations and policy, aligning information sharing with collaborative decision-making. Controlled experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains under constrained communication budgets, while three real-world experiments validate the framework in complex dual-robot tasks. These results highlight a shift from passive visual transmission toward active, task-oriented context sharing that directly supports collaborative decision-making.

title: Confidence-driven adaptive semantic transmission for task-oriented communication
authors: Suman Das; Prajnyajit Mohanty; Siddhartha S. Borkotoky
abstract: Image-based remote monitoring over wireless networks faces a trade-off between communication cost and classification reliability. Transmitting complete images is communication-intensive, whereas relying solely on lightweight edge classifiers may compromise accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose Confidence-Driven Adaptation (CDA) for image transmission and classification. An edge device (ED) captures images and applies a lightweight classifier before transmission to a remote server. Based on its classification confidence, the ED selects among three transmission modes with varying levels of information: a short text string reporting its predicted class when confidence is high, a compressed Region of Interest (ROI) at intermediate confidence levels, or an uncompressed ROI when confidence is low. The server accepts the predicted class directly in the first case and performs classification using a more powerful classifier in the other two cases. Numerical evaluations under bandwidth-limited, lossy links and latency-constrained settings demonstrate that CDA achieves high task accuracy at the receiver compared with non-adaptive baselines that transmit only the edge-classifier outcome or the uncompressed ROI.

title: TOFS: Feature Selection with Swap Supervision for Semantic Communication over Fading Channels
authors: Zhiyi Zhu; Eiji Takimoto; Patrick Finnerty; Chikara Ohta
abstract: Task-oriented semantic communication transmits task-relevant features to support receiver inference under limited communication resources and adverse channel conditions. For image classification, the usefulness of a feature depends on the other transmitted features and the distortion introduced by the wireless channel. Effective feature prioritization should therefore account for classification performance after transmission of the selected features. This paper proposes a Task-Oriented Feature Selection (\textit{TOFS}) framework and method, which evaluates feature replacements using receiver classification loss. Loss differences confirmed under independent transmission samples provide pairwise ranking supervision for a selector network. The trained selector predicts priorities in a single forward pass. CIFAR-10 simulations demonstrate improved classification accuracy over an importance-based feature selection baseline at the same transmitted feature count and average transmit power. The proposed \textit{TOFS} framework shows 84\% accuracy performance under Rayleigh fading and Gaussian noise, compared with the 68\% performance of a SOTA method.

title: Semantic Extraction Framework for Goal-Oriented V2X Communication Supporting Safe Intersection Passage
authors: Haoran Yang; Shan Lu; Takaya Yamazato
abstract: This paper proposes a transmitter-side semantic extraction framework for goal-oriented Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication supporting safe intersection passage. Instead of transmitting raw sensory data, roadside infrastructure extracts task-relevant semantic information from video and traffic-signal sequences and organizes them into compact semantic packets for low-latency driving-decision assistance. The intersection-passing problem is formulated as a set of traffic tasks under Japanese traffic regulations, and the proposed pipeline generates perception and intent semantics through object detection, object tracking, region-of-interest (ROI)-based semantic extraction, and recommended-action generation. The framework is implemented and evaluated on a self-constructed, CARLA-based single-vehicle dataset collected under clear weather conditions. Experimental results show high recommended-action accuracy within the tested task set, while the mean processing latency remains below the frame interval of the 15~fps input video.

title: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities
authors: Yalin E. Sagduyu; Tugba Erpek; Aylin Yener
abstract: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies. Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. The attack operates on intermediate communication representations subject to channel effects, with perturbations generated through a learned mapping applied at test time. It is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination. These results reveal a clear trade-off between SemCom gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, motivating the need for secure relay designs that account for insider threats.

title: Structured Agentic Learning for Persistent Spatial Acquisition in RDT-TAIS-Assisted Communications
authors: Bin Liu; Wei Ni; Tommy Svensson; Sofie Pollin
abstract: Persistent TAIS operation can reduce repeated radio-information acquisition by reusing environmental knowledge across control intervals. This knowledge changes with radio-environment evolution and current communication task. This paper studies persistent spatial knowledge maintenance for TAIS control and formulates it as a sequential information-acquisition problem that maximizes effective communication performance while accounting for physical-acquisition overhead under an outage-reliability constraint. We develop structured agentic spatial intelligence (ASI), which realizes a communication-oriented agent that maintains persistent spatial knowledge, forms beliefs from radio and context observations, and adapts physical information acquisition through closed-loop interaction with the radio environment. By jointly exploiting radio-consistent context inference, temporal knowledge-sufficiency assessment, graph-structured regional reasoning, and predictive outage-risk feedback, structured ASI determines when additional acquisition is needed, where it is directed, and how much physical information is sufficient before stopping or escalating to full radio-environment reacquisition. Numerical results show that structured ASI improves the effective rate by 2.59% while reducing acquisition overhead by 25.0% at six structural changes per 100 control intervals, and achieves a 2.82% effective-rate gain with a 41.8% overhead reduction over a heterogeneous 400-interval mission.

title: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Korean Language Learning: Applications, Challenges, and Instructional Strategies
authors: Yundong Wu
abstract: This conceptual narrative review examines the role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in Korean language learning. The paper synthesizes recent scholarship on AI-assisted language learning, Korean language education, technology acceptance, and educational ethics to develop an analytical framework for responsible classroom use. The review focuses on four dimensions: Korean language skills, Korean-specific linguistic and cultural features, instructional design, and governance risks. The analysis suggests that generative AI can support listening, speaking, reading, and writing when tasks are explicitly designed around Korean phonology, morphology, pragmatics, and learner purposes such as TOPIK preparation, study abroad, employment, and popular-culture engagement. It also identifies challenges in cultural-pragmatic accuracy, hallucinated expressions, assessment validity, data privacy, unequal access, teacher readiness, and learner dependency. The paper concludes that generative AI should function as a mediated learning resource rather than a substitute for teachers, learner judgment, or culturally grounded interaction.

title: Research on Attention Guidance and User Autonomy in AI-Powered Immersive Environments
authors: Mulin Qiao
abstract: As artificial intelligence gets deeply embedded into immersive environments, attention-guiding technology delivers ever more precise and efficient outcomes. Still, this improved efficiency carries an overlooked design risk: excessive AI guidance may steadily erode user agency and undermine exploratory behaviors as well as the process of meaning-making. This paper builds a critical conceptual framework to rethink attention-oriented design within AI-driven immersive settings. It defines excessive guidance and establishes theoretical links between this concept and three core facets of user agency: perceived control, voluntary choice and decision-making authority. Based on these findings, the paper calls for a paradigm shift from attention optimization to curiosity-led design. It also puts forward actionable behavioral measurement indicators covering exploration scope, average dwell time, path-following ratio, active choice frequency and recall test performance. The proposed framework supplies a new theoretical tool for human-computer interaction research in immersive scenarios and helps shift AI's role from a fixed route provider to an exploratory collaborator.

title: Antitrust Regulation of Algorithmic "Platform-Driven Involution'': From Governing the Corporate Person to Governing the Platform Ecosystem
authors: Sida Zeng
abstract: Digital platforms increasingly govern competition through algorithmically administered rules that allocate visibility, subsidies, commissions, participation opportunities, and sanctions. This article reconstructs ``platform-driven involution'' as a testable, portfolio-based theory-of-harm framework rather than a freestanding antitrust offense. Its application remains anchored in market definition, dominance, identified conduct under Article 22 of China's Anti-Monopoly Law, causal proof, competitive effects, and objective justification. The article clarifies that ecosystem analysis supplements rather than replaces relevant-market analysis and develops an evidence architecture for separating platform-induced effects from macroeconomic, demand, cost, and merchant-specific confounders. It then distinguishes preventive measures already supported by Chinese hard law or voluntary compliance guidance from compulsory competition-specific filing and pre-deployment assessment that would require clearer future authorization. The 2026 Trip.com decision is used to show how traffic allocation, exclusivity, lowest-price requirements, technical monitoring, and sanctions can form an integrated abuse architecture while liability remains tied to established statutory categories. Comparative analysis of EU platform regulation and Google Shopping supports calibrated procedural prevention, meaningful explanation, and causal discipline without protecting inefficient competitors or condemning aggressive competition.

title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
authors: Hongyu Xia
abstract: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-performance validation.

title: Screen use in children and adolescents: Developmental risks, benefits, and educational implications
authors: Hanna David
venue: Journal of Child Development, Exceptionality and Education
abstract: The “war against screens” — the intense parental and societal pushback against children’s and adolescents’ excessive use of smartphones, social media, tablets, and games — was lost from the outset. Modern life is inseparable from screens; even closed communities fail at total prohibition. Cross-national parent movements (Wait Until 8th, Smartphone Free Childhood) and policy responses (age restrictions, phone-free schools in Australia, Brazil, Europe, etc.) reflect these worries. Practical guidance centers on the Surgeon General’s “5 Ds” (Discuss, Do, Delay, Divert, Disconnect) and family media plans rather than prohibition. Historical roots of techno-skepticism are traced to Weizenbaum (1976) and Dreyfus. Part 2 focuses on doomscrolling (“catastrophe scrolling”) – compulsive consumption of distressing news. Evolutionary negativity bias, amygdala activation, and dopamine loops sustain the behavior. Gifted adolescents are particularly vulnerable due to intellectual hyperarousal, high empathy, and still-maturing self-regulation. Preliminary group interventions using gradual behavior shaping show promise in reducing the habit. Part 3 dismantles the popular notions of “brain rot” (Oxford Word of the Year 2024) and Spitzer’s “digital dementia.” Neither is a clinical entity; rigorous evidence for permanent cognitive atrophy from screen use is lacking. Content and context matter far more than the medium itself. Paradoxically, technology use in older adults is associated with lower cognitive-decline risk. Both terms remain useful only as red flags for problematic, addictive patterns that impair sleep, mood, and functioning. Overall, screens cannot be eliminated, but intentional limits, high-quality content, protected sleep, real-world activities, parental modeling, and platform accountability can substantially mitigate risks. The goal is not victory in a lost war, but wiser coexistence.

title: Instructional Reading Material Design and Use: Exploring the Roles of EFL Teachers’ Knowledge, Beliefs, and Contexts
authors: Nurul Fitriyah Almunawaroh
venue: SZTE Repository of Dissertations (University of Szeged)
abstract: Curriculum materials, such as textbooks, often provide limited cultural representation, contextual diversity, critical-thinking activities, and support for learner autonomy, which can negatively affect motivation and learning engagement. Thus, material adaptation is essential to meet the specific needs of different student groups and optimise learning. Teachers’ willingness and ease of adapting curriculum materials depend on their teaching beliefs and knowledge. Nevertheless, no previous study has investigated the overarching roles of teachers’ knowledge, beliefs, and contextual factors in shaping teachers’ curriculum material design and use. Therefore, this study aims to explore the roles of teachers’ technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK), pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), pedagogical beliefs, and contextual factors in shaping curriculum material design and use. This study is a mixed-method study with a convergent parallel design. Secondary high school English teachers were identified using snowball sampling to voluntarily participate in the quantitative part of the study (N = 257 and N = 251), and the qualitative part of the study (N = 6). A psychometrically validated TPACK-BPCKMU, open-ended survey, and interview collected data on teachers’ TPACK, PCK, beliefs, material use approach, contextual factors, and material design and use. The results of structural equation modelling show that teachers’ TPACK, PCK, and beliefs predicted curriculum material use approaches; beliefs mediated the predictive effect of TPACK and PCK on teachers’ material use approaches; and the interaction between TPACK and beliefs predicted material use approaches. Teachers’ DRM practices fall into four categories based on self-system beliefs and contextual factors. The findings suggest that teachers’ knowledge, beliefs, and context have interrelated roles in shaping how teachers design and use curriculum materials. Thus, continuous professional development programs that target improving teachers’ knowledge, identifying their beliefs, and fostering a constructivist orientation toward material design and use are essential, alongside efforts to reduce contextual barriers.

title: STEM E-MODULE DEVELOPMENT WITH DEMONSTRATION MEDIA FOR LINEAR MOTION
authors: Risva Maharani; Afrizal Mayub; Silvia Syeptiani
venue: University of Bengkulu Scholar Repository (University of Bengkulu)
abstract: This study aims to develop a STEM-based E-Practicum Module assisted by a line-follower robot demonstration to support junior high school students’ understanding of the concept of object motion. The study used the Research and Development (R&D) method with the 4D model, limited to the Development stage. A limited pilot test involving 30 seventh-grade students used a one-group pretest-posttest design. The results showed that the E-Practicum Module achieved a validity percentage of 91%, categorized as “highly valid,” and a readability score of 93%, categorized as “highly acceptable.” Students’ conceptual understanding improved after the implementation of the e-module, as indicated by an N-Gain score of 0.8696, categorized as “high.” Based on the measured indicators, the “identifying” indicator achieved the highest N-Gain value, while the “analyzing” indicator achieved the lowest N-Gain value. The novelty of this study lies in the integration of STEM-based laboratory activities with a line-follower robot demonstration within a single e-module to connect the concept of motion with physical phenomena that can be directly observed and measured. This integration provides a contextual learning experience that supports students in observing, measuring, and interpreting the concept of motion. The results of the study indicate that the developed E-Module for laboratory activities can be used as teaching material in the study of object motion in junior high school.

title: Edge Computing for IoT-Enabled Smart Cities: A Review of Middleware, Explainable AI, and User Behavior Analytics
authors: Alexandros Gazis; George Vavouras; Nikos E. Mastorakis; Kleanthi Santamouri; Nikolaos Pournaras; Stylianos Pappas
abstract: This review looks at cloud-IoT edge middleware for analyzing user behavior in smart cities, with a particular focus on linking behavioral analytics to energy-aware and mission-critical urban services. The topic sits at the crossroads of smart-city platforms, IoT sensing, edge/fog/cloud computing, service-oriented architectures, machine learning, explainable AI, privacy-aware governance, and energy-critical applications such as EV charging, energy demand, environmental exposure, crowd safety, and the operational resilience of urban infrastructure. As such, this paper maps out the main categories of user-behavior data, examines five application domains, compares several case studies, and puts forward a new XAI-EdgeSOA Middleware Framework called X-EdgeCity Middleware. This framework brings together IoT sensing, edge preprocessing, fog coordination, event-driven communication, cloud analytics, XAI explanations, privacy-by-design, and benchmark logging. The goal is to support not just general smart-city applications, but also energy-sensitive or mission-critical services, where latency, reliability, explainability, and accountability have a direct impact on urban safety and continuity of operations.

title: Reference-Dependent Utility Optimization for Goal-Oriented Communication Systems
authors: Symeon Vaidanis; Photios A. Stavrou; Marios Kountouris
abstract: Traditional communication resource allocation optimizes operational metrics such as rate, latency, energy efficiency, and reliability. Motivated by goal-oriented semantic communication, we develop a generalized allocation framework that transforms operational rewards through reference-dependent user utilities and evaluates them via expected utility, cumulative prospect theory (CPT), or related decision criteria. The formulation separates operational rewards, user-side valuations, and system-level decision criteria under uncertainty. We characterize utilities incorporating QoS/service reference levels, deficit sensitivity, post-reference saturation, and loss aversion. Weighted sum-reward maximization, proportional fairness, $α$-fairness, and stochastic expected utility maximization emerge as exact special cases, while soft QoS-aware allocation follows from a deficit-penalty generalization. For deterministic orthogonal systems, we derive utility-weighted marginal-reward KKT conditions characterizing global optimality under concave composite objectives. For nonorthogonal and stochastic systems, we develop successive convex approximation (SCA) algorithms and establish stationary-point guarantees under explicit smooth and composite nonsmooth assumptions, including a CPT branch-stationarity result under eventual nondegenerate ordering identification. For globally solved penalized problems, we derive an $O(1/λ)$ bound on excess aggregate soft-QoS deficit, and on the deficit itself whenever a QoS-feasible allocation exists. Additionally, we establish an $O(1/ε^2)$ outer iteration bound for the smooth fixed-step SCA best-response residual. Numerical examples demonstrate how reference points, marginal utility slopes, channel quality, and resource budgets influence active users and allocation policies.

title: Operational Indirect Rate-Distortion Functions for Classification Tasks
authors: Yann Miguet; Elsa Dupraz; Philippe Mary
abstract: In goal-oriented communications, indirect source coding involves two sources: a semantic source $X$ and an observation $Z$, which is the only source available at the encoder. In this paper, we consider this framework for classification, where the decoder only needs to reconstruct $X$. We argue that the gap between the indirect rate-distortion function and the performance of practical learned coding schemes, such as variational information bottleneck (VIB) and variational autoencoder (VAE) architectures, comes from three effects: the latent representation, the choice of the deep neural network (DNN) architecture and training loss, and whether the encoder is aware of the task. To quantify these effects, we introduce four operational rate-distortion functions that account for the DNN architecture and the training loss, and we establish a hierarchy among them. We then derive these functions for a Gaussian mixture source, where $X$ is the mixture state. Numerical results, both for the Gaussian mixture and for practical coding schemes on the CIFAR-100 dataset, quantify the rate loss incurred by each effect.

title: On the Optimality of Implicit Feedback in Markov Decision Processes over Imperfect Links
authors: Romain Planchon; Federico Chiariotti; Federico Mason; Andrea Zanella; Deniz Gunduz
abstract: Goal-oriented communication protocols are explicitly designed to support the objectives of target applications, such as the monitoring and control of remote processes, while minimizing data traffic. This study considers a transmitter node that observes the environment state and sends it to a remote agent, which then performs control actions. This problem can be modeled as a remote Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), a subclass of decentralized POMDPs. Existing studies limit transmissions through communication costs, but neglect the effect of channel impairments and non-ideal or delayed feedback. In this work, we study the optimal joint transmission and control policies over lossy forward channels without explicit acknowledgments. We introduce \emph{revealing} policies, under which the receiver's action, observed directly by the transmitter, discloses the outcome of the forward transmission, keeping the two agents synchronized without a feedback channel. We derive sufficient conditions for the optimality of time-invariant policies in this implicit feedback regime for general POMDPs, along with strictly weaker sufficient conditions in the special case of contextual bandits. Our simulations over a family of remote POMDPs show that these conditions are conservative, and revealing policies are optimal over a substantially wider parameter range than the conditions warrant.
