title: Is this correct? How Perceived Inaccuracies Shape Museum Visitors' Engagement with a Virtual Expert
authors: Marcus Winter; Phil Blume
venue: University of Brighton Repository (University of Brighton)
abstract: This paper examines museum visitors' perceptions of inaccuracies in the responses of a conversational agent, cast as a virtual expert on the history and architecture of a heritage building, and how they shape their engagement and learning. It discusses the curatorial need addressed by the agent, its technical design and implementation, and its empirical evaluation with visitors to the building. Findings show that visitors engaged extensively with the agent and appreciated the direct access to expertise, despite expressing a preference for human interaction. Most participants reported that the agent helped them to learn about the building's history and architecture. While many qualified this by expressing doubts about the provided information, perceived inaccuracies also provided opportunities for deeper engagement and independent inquiry. The highly rated user experience, potential for learning, and open, low-energy, privacy-preserving technical design strongly align with curatorial goals. The paper's main contribution, empirical findings on how perceived inaccuracies affect visitor's engagement and learning, is relevant for practitioners and researchers designing conversational agents in heritage contexts.

title: English as a Foreign Language Instructors’ Professional Identity and Professional Development in Higher Education Institutions
authors: Hijjatul Qamariah
venue: SZTE Repository of Dissertations (University of Szeged)
abstract: Teacher Professional identity (TPI) and professional development (PD) are key constructs for the quality of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction in higher education. However, research in non Western contexts often lacks conceptual clarity and methodological depth in explaining how these constructs emerge and interact. Guided by a sociocultural perspective that views identity as socially constructed, negotiated, and shaped through participation in institutional practices, this study examines how Indonesian EFL instructors construct their professional identities and how these identities influence their teaching practice and engagement in professional development. An exploratory sequential mixed methods design was employed. The qualitative phase involved semi structured interviews (N = 10) and ego centered network cards (N = 11) to capture instructors’ lived experiences and the relational influences shaping their identities. Thematic analysis identified five themes: professional identity construction, professional development practices, pedagogical agency, institutional influence, emotional and relational dimensions. These themes informed the development of a survey instrument, which was validated and administered to 161 instructors across diverse higher education institutions. The quantitative phase used correlation analysis to examine associations among validated constructs: teaching practice, pedagogical knowledge, reflective practice, institutional support, and professional development. This was followed by multiple regression analyses to determine the extent to which TPI predicted these outcomes. The results showed strong correlations among all constructs. Multiple regression analysis showed that mentorship emerged as the strongest predictor (β = .473, p < .001), indicating that instructors who receive meaningful guidance and peer support tend to report stronger professional identities. Self directed learning also significantly predicted identity strength (β = .395, p < .001), suggesting that instructors who actively engage in autonomous learning and skill development tend to construct stronger professional identities. Institutional support also contributed significantly (β = .344, p < .001), demonstrating that supportive institutional contexts foster stronger professional identity formation. Teaching experience was not a significant predictor of professional identity (β = .026, p = .336), suggesting the accumulation of teaching experience alone does s not automatically result in a more developed professional identity. Regression analysis further showed that PI significantly predicted teaching practice and engagement in PD, suggesting that identity plays a substantial role in shaping professional behavior rather than merely reflecting accumulated experience. While professional development contributes to identity formation, the findings suggest that identity exerts a stronger influence on instructors’ developmental choices and instructional decisions, pointing to a reciprocal but asymmetrical relationship. This study contributes to the field in three main ways: (1) by offering a contextually grounded conceptualization of EFL instructor identity in Indonesian higher education; (2) by providing a validated measurement instrument that may support future research and policy-related work and (3) by presenting empirical evidence of the important role of identity in shaping teaching practice and sustained professional development. The findings underscore the importance of institutional environments that recognize the dynamic nature of teacher identity and provide meaningful, long term support for professional growth.

title: Transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation at Yintang attenuates nap-deprivation-induced working memory decline: parallel associations with prefrontal activation and cardiac vagal tone
authors: Fan Jh; Liang Wang; Ze Lv; Chengfei Li; Yikai Pan; Yuan Wang; Shuhan Li; Yongchun Wang; Yuan Gao; Xiqing Sun
abstract: Abstract Background ​ Working memory (WM) decrement due to circadian dips and sleep restriction is a prevalent issue among interns, potentially impacting clinical decision-making. Non-invasive neuromodulation techniques, such as transcutaneous electrical acupoint stimulation (TEAS), offer a promising approach to mitigate cognitive fatigue. This study investigates the efficacy and underlying neurophysiological mechanism of TEAS at the Yintang (EX-HN3) acupoint in counteracting WM impairment induced by nap deprivation. Methods We enrolled 90 interns with habitual napping behavior, who were randomly assigned to one of three groups: normal control group (NC), nap deprivation group (ND), and nap deprivation group receiving TEAS intervention (ND+TEAS). Cognitive performance was assessed using a 3-back WM task at baseline (12:00) and post-intervention (15:00). Concurrently, prefrontal cerebral hemodynamics and autonomic nervous system activity were monitored via functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and heart rate variability (HRV), respectively. Subjective cognitive load was evaluated using the NASA-Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). Results Compared to the NC group, the ND group exhibited significant deterioration in WM accuracy and speed, accompanied by reduced prefrontal cortex (PFC) activation and attenuated parasympathetic activity (reflected by decreased HRV high-frequency power). The ND+TEAS group demonstrated a reversal of these effects, showing superior WM performance, enhanced PFC oxygenation, and increased vagally-mediated HRV indices relative to the ND group. Crucially, mediation analysis revealed that the improvement in WM performance following TEAS was mediated by its effect on augmenting PFC activation, which in turn was associated with increased parasympathetic tone. Conclusions TEAS at the Yintang acupoint effectively alleviates nap deprivation-induced WM impairment. The mechanism appears to involve the enhancement of parasympathetic nervous activity and the subsequent facilitation of prefrontal cortical function. These findings provide novel experimental evidence for the brain-heart interaction as a pathway for cognitive enhancement and position TEAS as a viable, non-invasive strategy to bolster cognitive resilience in populations susceptible to circadian fatigue, such as clinical staff.

title: ImpCresst: a versatile simulation tool focusing on solid-state detectors at keV energies
authors: G. Angloher; S. Banik; A. Bento; A. Bertolini; Robert Breier; C. Bucci; J. Burkhart; L. Burmeister; L. Canonica; F. Casadei; E. Cipelli; S. Di Lorenzo; J. Dohm; F. Dominsky; A. Erb; E. Fascione; F. von Feilitzsch; S. Fichtinger; D. Fuchs; A. Fuss; V. M. Ghete; P. Gorla; P.V. Guillaumon; D. Hauff; M. Ješkovský; J. Jochum; M. Kaznacheeva; H. Kluck; H. Kraus; B. von Krosigk; A. Langenkämper; M. Mancuso; B. Mauri; Valentyna M. Mokina; C. Moore; P. Murali; M. Olmi; T. Ortmann; C. Pagliarone; L. Pattavina; F. Petricca; W. Potzel; P. Povinec; F. Pröbst; F. Pucci; F. Reindl; J. Rothe; K. Schäffner; J. Schieck; S. Schönert; C. Schwertner; M. Stahlberg; L. Stodolsky; Christian Strandhagen; R. Strauss; F. Toschi; I. Usherov; D. Valdenaire; M. Zanirato; Vanessa Zema
abstract: Abstract We present Imp Cresst , a Geant4 -based Monte Carlo tool to simulate backgrounds from natural and cosmogenic radionuclides, and calibration signals in solid-state detectors and their response to it. It is tuned for a fast-evolving and heterogeneous detector environment with a focus on physics at the keV range. This tool was originally developed and validated by the CRESST collaboration; however, its flexibility and configurability make it suitable for other experiments with similar requirements. Key features of Imp Cresst include the dynamic geometry implementation directly from CAD files, ROOT-based data persistency of the whole event topology and automatic metadata annotation for data provenance, and interfaces to various particle generators, particularly for radiogenic and cosmogenic radionuclides. It includes also a newly developed particle generator for radioactive bulk and surface contaminations which is completely independent of any user defined confinement volumes. The auxiliary tool CresstDS applies detector-specific energy and time resolution based on a user-provided data set of empirical parameterization. We discuss also how to manage an Imp Cresst based workflow in an HPC environment based on Apptainer and nextflow.

title: Low Latency Gaze Tracking via Latent Optical Sensing
authors: Yidan Zheng; Matheus Souza; Kaizhang Kang; Qiang Fu; Hadi Amata; Wolfgang Heidrich
abstract: We present a real-time gaze tracking system that directly acquires task-relevant latent features using a fully passive optical encoder. Instead of forming and processing full-resolution images, our approach leverages a microlens array with a co-designed binary chromium mask to perform spatially multiplexed optical encoding, producing a compact set of measurements sufficient for gaze estimation. By integrating sensing and feature extraction in the optical domain, the proposed system eliminates the need for high-bandwidth image readout and substantially reduces computational overhead. The encoded measurements are captured by a 4 x 4 phototransistor array and mapped to gaze direction using a lightweight neural network. Our proof-of-concept prototype enables an end-to-end sensing-to-inference latency of 3.4 ms, outperforming published research systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both simulated and real-world data, achieving competitive gaze estimation accuracy while significantly reducing end-to-end latency compared to conventional camera-based pipelines. The proposed system establishes a new operating point in the accuracy-latency-compute trade-off for latency- and resource-constrained gaze tracking. This work highlights the potential of task-driven optical sensing for ultra-low-latency, computationally efficient human-computer interaction systems.

title: SiZeUp: Fast 3D Proxy from Aerial Images via Depth Ordinal Loss
authors: Wenjun Zhou; Yunshan Li; Qiaoyu Zhu; Weidan Xiong; Hao Y. Zhang; Daniel Cohen‐Or; Hui Huang
abstract: We present SiZeUp, a fast and scalable approach for constructing large-scale 3D urban proxy models directly from calibrated oblique aerial imagery. Our method adopts a height-from-footprint representation, reducing 3D building abstraction to a low-dimensional optimization problem in which building footprints are extruded by a single height parameter. To enable efficient and robust height estimation, we introduce an ordinal depth consistency loss that enforces agreement between the relative depth ordering of rendered proxies and depth priors predicted by a monocular depth model. This is realized through a differentiable renderer that maps parametric building proxies into multi-view depth images, allowing gradients to be propagated from depth supervision to building heights. Our ordinal formulation produces stable optimization in practice and avoids explicit feature matching or dense point cloud reconstruction. Rather than relying on metric depth, which can be unreliable under monocular scale ambiguity, our ordinal depth consistency loss operates on relative depths, providing a more reliable signal across views. Combined with an efficient dynamic view selection, our approach achieves a 23-52$\times$ speedup over state-of-the-art proxy reconstruction pipelines while maintaining comparable proxy-level coverage and volume consistency, making it well suited for large-scale urban modeling tasks.

title: Uncertainty DMD: Restoring Diversity in Few-Step Autoregressive Video Distillation
authors: Zixuan Duan; Xunzhi Xiang; Yabo Chen; Xin Zhang; Changhan Liu; Haibin Huang; Chi Zhang; Qi Fan; Xuelong Li
abstract: Few-step distillation improves the efficiency of autoregressive (AR) video generation, but often causes diversity collapse: under the same prompt, different noise samples tend to produce highly similar videos with weakened motion dynamics. We analyze this degradation in Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD)-distilled AR video generators and find that, in the autoregressive setting, it takes the form of a structured uncertainty collapse: the mode-seeking bias of DMD maps different noise samples to nearly identical first chunks, and the deterministic AR cache then propagates this collapsed state to all subsequent chunks, turning a local loss of stochasticity at the rollout root into a global suppression of temporal variation. Based on this analysis, we propose Uncertainty DMD, a simple uncertainty-injection framework that restores stochasticity at two key stages of AR generation: a timestep perturbation for the first chunk to increase first-chunk diversity, and a stochastic cache-writing mechanism for later chunks to preserve uncertainty in autoregressive conditioning. The method requires no architectural changes and introduces only lightweight perturbation operations. The same perturbation mechanisms are used during both training and inference. Experiments show that Uncertainty DMD consistently improves diversity and motion dynamics while maintaining comparable per-sample visual quality.

title: CGGT: Curve-Grounded Geometry Transformer for 3D Parametric Curve Reconstruction
authors: Zhirui Gao; Renjiao Yi; Yunfan Ye; Ruizhen Hu; Chenyang Zhu; Wei Chen; Kai Xu
abstract: Recovering editable 3D parametric curves from 2D images is a fundamental challenge in computer graphics, bridging pixel-based perception and vector-based CAD modeling. Existing NeRF- and 3DGS-based methods often rely on dense calibrated views, precomputed 2D edge maps, and costly per-scene optimization, limiting their applicability to casually captured real-world inputs. We propose CGGT, a Curve-Grounded Geometry Transformer that directly grounds 3D-consistent 2D curve instances in the image space from sparse, unposed multi-view images. CGGT combines a geometry-aware transformer encoder for multi-view feature learning with a curve-aware masked-attention decoder for cross-view instance association. In a single forward pass, it predicts camera parameters, dense depth maps, and instance-level 2D curve masks, which are then lifted into 3D and refined through a fast parametric optimization stage to recover compact, editable 3D curve primitives. To support structured curve learning, we introduce Wireframe-100K, a large-scale dataset comprising 100,000 CAD models with diverse topologies, realistic multi-view renderings, and accurate parametric curve annotations. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves substantial improvements in both reconstruction accuracy and efficiency, particularly under challenging sparse-view settings and in separating persistent 3D structural edges from view-dependent image edges caused by silhouettes, textures, and appearance variations. Despite being trained solely on synthetic data, CGGT generalizes well to real-world images, demonstrating its potential for practical CAD-style wireframe reconstruction from unconstrained visual inputs.

title: Improving Zero-shot 3D Semantic Mapping in Offroad with Geometric Priors
authors: Eerik Alamikkotervo; Risto Ojala
abstract: Semantic 3D mapping is a powerful representation that enables platform agnostic mobile robot navigation in challenging offroad conditions. Current vision foundation models can accurately predict semantics zero-shot on structured scenes but performance is compromised in natural environments. On the other hand, 3D point clouds encode valuable information for discriminating semantics in scenarios where vision foundation models fail. In this work, we propose fitting a sphericity-elevation distribution for each semantic class to act as geometric anchor. Only the points with the most confident vision foundation model predictions are considered when fitting to produce high quality geometric prior distributions. The geometric prior is fused with the vision foundation model prediction to produce the final semantic mapping. The proposed prior improves SAM3 baseline by +6.3 in mIoU and +8.9 in accuracy on the RELLIS-3D dataset, and by +1.7 in mIoU and +2.1 in accuracy on the WildScenes dataset. The source code will be made public upon paper acceptance.

title: ALIVE: Bring Foundation Features to Life with Events
authors: Rong Zou; Haiqing Hao; Davide Scaramuzza
abstract: Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder. We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation. Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200,ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9,mAP in detection, 11.6,mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.

title: Why Multi-Source Audio Fails to Compose: A Geometric Diagnosis and Its Remedy
authors: Anurag Singh; Prajwal Singh; Shanmuganathan Raman
abstract: Multi-source audio-to-image generation exhibits consistent compositional failures when audio tokens occupy geometrically displaced, semantically unanchored positions in the CLIP text-token space, where the diffusion U-Net lacks the prior to reliably attend to them or ground them in distinct spatial regions. We formalize this as the geometric displacement phenomenon and expose it through a two-level clustering analysis comparing BEATs and CLAP embeddings at the raw encoder and projected CLIP token levels. Three geometric properties emerge as important: intra-class compactness, angular alignment with the CLIP text manifold, and inter-token spatial separation. We show that CLAP, whose contrastive language-audio pretraining aligns embeddings with natural language semantics, substantially outperforms BEATs on all three properties, improving the silhouette score by more than 3x and the Audio-Image Content score as well. Building on this analysis, we introduce a multi-token extension that requires no diffusion-backbone retraining and assigns each audio source to a distinct placeholder token in the CLIP tokenizer, complemented by a mixed inference-time objective that combines Attend-and-Excite with an A* spatial separation loss to resolve residual cross-token interference. For evaluation, we construct multi-audio compositional benchmarks from VGGSound (VGG2, VGG3, and VGGN) and extend six standard audio-image metrics to the multi-source setting. Across five benchmarks and four strong baselines, our method achieves strong results on the metrics most directly tied to compositional faithfulness, with AIC improvements of up to 2.25x over the strongest baseline and FID reduced by nearly 2x on two-source generation. We propose geometric displacement as a diagnostic framework for cross-modal generation systems that project learned embeddings into a pretrained contrastive space.

title: CoT-WAM: Collaborative Training of Vision-Language Models and World-Action Models via Plan Latents
authors: Jinhao Zhang; Yushen Zuo; Ke Rui; Weitao Zhou; Haibao Yu; Honglong Tian; Xiaoheng Ma; Jie Mei; Jiawei Wang; Minglei Li
abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments.

title: A Dual-SOM Learner Model of Instructional Efficiency within Cognitive Load Theory
authors: Spyridon Revithis
abstract: This paper presents a novel methodological framework, integrating a dual self-organising map (SOM) neural network architecture with Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), for assessing instructional efficiency within learning environments. By representing curriculum content as a directed acyclic graph of topic dependencies, the proposed model captures collective learning behaviour across two core dimensions: academic performance and subjective/introspective mental effort. During SOM training, representative data sets of successful learner trajectories are compressed into two topologically ordered, identically structured neural networks: PSOM (performance space) and ESOM (mental effort space). By pairing these behavioural maps, the model serves as a decision-support tool that enables instructors to simultaneously pinpoint structural instructional design defects, such as hidden topic prerequisites, and evaluate collective cognitive load profiles. The implementation and performance of the PSOM component (and, by extension, its symmetrical twin, ESOM) is linked to an earlier modelling study employing a SOM with identical structure and encoding semantics situated in the same domain (i.e., a learning environment). This paper combines the study of behavioural phenomena with theoretical work on human cognitive architecture via SOM neurocomputational cognitive behavioural modelling.

title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation
authors: Michael Schwarz; Zhendong Ang; Umang Mathur
abstract: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.

title: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
authors: Ilia Karpov; Andrey Atamanyuk; Dmitry Ilvovsky; Aleksandr Anokhin; Alex Elizov; Dmitry Zagorulkin; Sergei O. Kuznetsov
abstract: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it. T/E/S combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Across reasoning and information-seeking tasks, events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for Qwen with LoRA. Span duration and preceding events are associated with transitions, and retaining event history across span boundaries improves prediction. We formulate budget-allocation counting and action-conditional continuation queries, prove counting hardness under explicit encodings, and derive conditions for affordable decision certification. In finite-process experiments, bounds that cancel shared continuation mass recover the same optimal actions as full dynamic programming while reducing mean inference CPU time by 77.7%. On 71 held-out HotpotQA and MuSiQue questions, a compact structural observer improves prediction of whether a fixed inference procedure finishes within a CPU allowance: Brier loss falls from 0.0836 to 0.0756. An annotation audit identifies substantial errors in that observer, separating this computational result from semantic validation of its features.

title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
authors: Abdiaziz Muse; Jiju Poovvancheri
abstract: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.

title: AnalogMorph: evaluating representation fidelity in LLM analog netlist reasoning
authors: Wei Zhen Leong; Steve Gunn; Jing Huey Khor
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted to augment analog integrated circuit design, yet existing studies primarily evaluate circuit recognition accuracy on canonical representations while largely overlooking representation fidelity. In analog design, electrically identical circuits may be represented using arbitrary device indices, net names, transistor ordering, and structural decompositions. Human designers recognize these representations as equivalent, yet LLM behavior under such transformations is not well characterized. This work introduces AnalogMorph, a metamorphic benchmark applying three topology-preserving transformations (device-net permutation, both constructive and deceptive semantic keyword injection) to curated topologies. The benchmark evaluates whether circuit interpretations remain consistent when electrical connectivity is unchanged. The suitability of a structure-aware encoding based on the device–net incidence matrix with breadth-first electrical position ordering is further examined. Within the evaluated settings, experimental results reveal substantial sensitivity of contemporary LLMs to electrically irrelevant textual cues. Although structure-aware representations can alter model behavior, their benefits are highly model-dependent, indicating that representation engineering alone does not guarantee robust circuit understanding. These findings position AnalogMorph as a diagnostic complement to recognition accuracy for evaluating representation-robust and trustworthy analog design assistants.

title: TICK: Text-Informed Contrastive Kernels for Probabilistic Time-Series Retrieval
authors: Rayen Ben Masseoud; Faïcel Chamroukhi
abstract: The coexistence of sensor data and textual knowledge across industrialapplications highlights the need to align natural language withmultivariate time series. This challenge is typically treated as adeterministic task, ignoring the fact that a vague query may matchhundreds of recordings while a precise one matches only a few. We arguethat text-to-time-series retrieval is inherently a probabilisticcross-modal problem and propose TICK, a framework in which each textquery carries a learned uncertainty $\sigma_t$ reflecting how many timeseries are semantically compatible with it. Without supervising $\sigma_t$directly, we find that it tracks query specificity with Spearmancorrelations $\rho \in [-0.88, -0.75]$ on three independent industrialbenchmarks. We further show that coupling the time-series representationto the text query is a necessary condition for this calibration to emerge:without it, $\sigma_t$ collapses to a constant, eliminating the model'sability to adapt its retrieval scope to query specificity. Because$\sigma_t$ sets the retrieval scope of a query, TICK spends a query-dependentcandidate budget instead of a fixed worst-case one, on top of a frozen33M-parameter sentence encoder and a small patch Transformer, with no languagemodel in the inference loop.

title: Exploring multimodal AI--XR interactions for software development: From expert perspectives to semantic code outlines
authors: Ilya Zakharov; Alexey Markin; Konstantin Ostroukhov; Alexey Perminov; Roham Koohestani; Ekaterina Koshchenko; Agnia Sergeyuk
abstract: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

title: Leveraging Binary Hashing for Scalable Index Assignment in Semantic Communications
authors: Leonardo Roque; Kuangyun Zhu; Louis-Adrien Dufrène; Quentin Lampin; Grégoire Lefebvre; Mohamad Assaad
abstract: Transmitting semantically structured embedding vectors over digital channels is costly in bit rate, while conven- tional vector quantization approaches face limitations in scalabil- ity, encoding complexity, and index assignment. This paper inves- tigates binary hashing techniques from the information retrieval literature as semantic indexing strategies for general-purpose networks. We study random Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) along with Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-, Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA)-, and ITQ (Iterative Quantization)- based variants in a semantic communication pipeline over a Binary Symmetric Channel. Embeddings are compressed into binary codes, reconstructed through Hamming retrieval from a shared table, and evaluated on downstream classification. Ex- periments on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) and the Banking77 dataset show that data-dependent hashing improves upon random LSH, while ITQ refinement increases robustness to channel noise. Among the evaluated methods, CCA- ITQ achieves the best classification accuracy across the tested channel conditions. These results indicate that binary hashing is an efficient and scalable alternative to quantization-based embedding compression for semantic communications.

title: Recursive Spectral Graph Partitioning Coding for Index Assignment in Semantic Communications
authors: Leonardo Roque; Louis-Adrien Dufrène; Quentin Lampin; Grégoire Lefebvre; Mohamad Assaad
abstract: Transmitting quantized semantic embeddings over a bit-flip channel requires a binary mapping that minimizes expected reconstruction distortion. The classical Binary Switching Algorithm (BSA) ($\mathcal{O}(K^3 \log K)$ for $K$ centroids) yields locally optimal assignments but ignores hierarchical bit significance, making it incompatible with Unequal Error Protection (UEP). We propose Recursive Spectral Graph Partitioning (RSGP), which recursively bisects the centroid affinity graph along the Fiedler eigenvector so that early bits separate semantically distant groups while later bits refine local structure. RSGP runs in $\mathcal{O}(K^3)$ with no iterative outer loop, and is the only method studied to show a systematic positive UEP gain: protecting early bits over later ones improves accuracy for RSGP, while being neutral or harmful for unstructured assignments. Experiments on the Banking77 dataset and the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) confirm that RSGP consistently matches or exceeds BSA accuracy across codebook sizes and error profiles.

title: Scaling Channel-Adaptive Self-Supervised Learning
authors: Alice V. De Lorenci; Seungeun Yi; Theo Moutakanni; Piotr Bojanowski; Camille Couprie; Juan C. Caicedo; Wolfgang M. Pernice
abstract: Recent advances in self-supervised pre-training of foundation models for natural images have made them a popular choice for various visual systems and applications. Self-supervised strategies are also promising in non-RGB scientific imaging domains such as in biology, medical and satellite imagery, but their broader application is hampered by heterogeneity in channel composition and semantics between relevant datasets: two datasets may contain different numbers of channels, and these may reveal distinct aspects of an object or scene. Recent works on channel adaptive strategies report substantial advantages for those that account for variable channel compositions without sacrificing the ability to jointly encode channels; yet, how these strategies behave at scale remains unclear. We here show that, surprisingly, trained across large-scale datasets, independent-encoding of channels outperforms joint-encoding methods by a substantial margin. We validate this result along an extensive set of experiments on various datasets from cell microscopy to geospatial imagery. Our DINO BoC approach sets a new state-of-the-art across challenging benchmarks, including generalization to out-of-distribution tasks and unseen channel combinations. We open-source code and model weights for a new general-purpose feature extractor for fluorescent microscopy.

title: QVS-LIVO RiskMap: Health- and Information-Aware View Selection for Multi-Camera LIVO and Off-Road Risk Mapping
authors: Zihan Pan; Jinghan Wang; Hang Li; Feng Cheng; Tianchen Liu; Gaoliang Peng
abstract: Multi-camera observations in off-road environments vary significantly in reliability, posing challenges when complementing degraded geometric constraints. Motivated by this, we propose Quality-aware View Selection Lidar-Vision Odometry Risk Mapping (QVS-LIVO RiskMap), which decouples visual processing for state estimation from that for semantic mapping. The front end evaluates camera observations through read-only pretracking on a shared lidar-inertial posterior, combining observation health with geometric complementarity. Channel health memory and switching hysteresis govern selection of at most one eligible view for direct photometric correction. The posterior is retained when no view is eligible or the correction fails acceptance. The mapping back end integrates semantic observations from all available views in a shared world grid. Vehicle-scale geometry constrains semantic risk corrections, while spatial and temporal evidence supports risk confirmation. The system also produces a local bird's-eye-view (BEV) risk map and a global 2.5D semantic-terrain risk map with obstacle instance voxels. On two field sequences, QVS-LIVO achieved horizontal root mean square errors of 0.910 m and 1.664 m. It reduced error by 43.3% relative to FAST-LIO2 on the degraded long-route sequence. Across 12 controlled camera-fault configurations involving dropout, black frames and 60 ms timestamp shifts, it maintained complete trajectories with errors of 1.54-2.23 m. When deployed onboard an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the system generates local and global maps at 9.94 Hz and 2.00 Hz, respectively, with a median local mapping latency of 32.4 ms. These runtime results demonstrate the real-time feasibility of selective visual state updates alongside multi-view semantic mapping under challenging off-road conditions. The code and related resources are available at: https://github.com/zihanPan-HIT/QVS-LIVO.

title: BiRefNet-V2: Rethinking Bilateral Reference for High-Resolution Dichotomous Image Segmentation
authors: Peng Zheng; Deng-Ping Fan; Binglu Wang; Nicu Sebe
abstract: Dichotomous image segmentation requires pixel-accurate foreground-background separation while preserving fine structures such as thin filaments, sharp edges, and intricate textures. BiRefNet addressed this challenge through bilateral references, combining image patches and gradient information, but its inward reference loses local spatial structure and lacks semantic guidance, while its outward reference relies on single-channel gradient attention. We recast this paradigm as controlled information recovery - locality determines what spatial information survives, semantic selectivity what information enters, and focused boundary supervision where refinement occurs - and propose BiRefNet-V2 to implement it: (1) locality-preserving and semantically guided detail injection through space-to-depth transformation, overlapping patches, and a Semantically Guided Gate; (2) a learned boundary stream with focused supervision that generates full-channel residual attention without requiring boundary annotations; and (3) a dual-branch decoder integrating depth-wise boundary convolutions with large-kernel attention. A modernized framework - LayerNorm, GELU, the Lion optimizer, and a DINOv3 backbone - cuts training from 600 to 50 epochs. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on DIS5K, camouflaged object detection, and high-resolution salient object detection across all 13 evaluation sets. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet-V2.

title: Monitoring One Channel Is Not Communication Control: Causal Evidence for Adaptive Reallocation of Joint Message--Route Codes
authors: Liu Hung Ming; Tian Xia
abstract: Monitoring a visible channel can change how learned agents communicate without removing why communication is useful. We test this distinction in an end-to-end game where a sender and receiver learn a discrete protocol and route policy without communication supervision. In two independent 20-seed batches, 20/20 and 19/20 protocols form. Online partial coverage increases shadow-route share over no monitoring by .701 [.574,.826] and .575 [.412,.737], while task accuracy remains .905/.913 and signed frozen message contribution remains .592/.563. Complete coverage removes most selective migration without removing communication. Frozen interventions, including a fresh pre-outcome confirmation, show that route is semantic: joint message--route shuffling changes .668 of receiver predictions and route alone retains .388 accuracy versus .25 chance. A corrected explicit-silence cost makes 18/20 policies fully silent and lowers mean sending to .050, but its strict complete-suppression gate fails because two seeds retain communication. Failed semantic-evasion and operational gates further bound the result. The evidence supports adaptive reallocation of a joint message--route code under partial monitoring, not open-world route discovery, emergent encryption, or a universal defense.

title: Computational Studies of Triplet State Formation in Zinc Dipyrrin Complexes
authors: Reuben Kwabla Adigbli
venue: Digital Commons - East Tennessee State University (East Tennessee State University)
abstract: Zinc dipyrromethene complexes are promising earth-abundant photosensitizers due to their strong visible-light absorption and tunable excited states. To rationally design them for photocatalysis and photodynamic therapy, a molecular-level understanding of triplet-state formation is needed, but details of intersystem crossing remain unclear. To study the effect of π-extension, we synthesized an indole-substituted zinc dipyrrin complex: the dipyrromethane ligand was prepared from indole and mesitaldehyde, oxidized to the dipyrromethene, then coordinated with zinc. DFT and TD-DFT calculations determined ground and excited-state geometries and energies in different solvents, modeled absorption spectra, and visualized charge distributions. The results show how solvent polarity shifts energies of the ground, lowest triplet, and excited singlet states, and influences charge separation in the excited state. These computational findings, coupled with photophysical measurements, will establish a framework for designing zinc dipyrrin complexes with improved triplet state yield.

title: Markov Decision Process-based Real-time Navigation for Autonomous Aerial Vehicles Using Video
authors: Khizar Anjum; Parul Pandey; Vidyasagar Sadhu; Roberto Tron; Dario Pompili
abstract: Abstract Autonomous aerial vehicle navigation is critical for applications ranging from search and rescue operations to warehouse automation, requiring real-time decision-making under severe computational and power constraints. While traditional geometric approaches using 3D point clouds provide accurate navigation, they impose prohibitive computational overhead for resource-constrained drones, and existing computer vision algorithms for semantic navigation create a fundamental performance bottleneck where static parameter configurations fail to adapt to varying environmental conditions. This paper addresses this gap through a novel Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework that dynamically optimizes object detection parameters based on input characteristics, intelligently selecting algorithm configurations from both feature-based (HoG/Edgeboxes with SVMs) and neural network (CNN) detection pipelines while utilizing classifier confidence scores as quality indicators. Comprehensive evaluation across KUL traffic sign datasets, custom BU-RU drone-collected footage, and hardware-in-the-loop AirSim simulations demonstrates significant performance improvements: 20-70% execution time reduction while maintaining 98-100% detection accuracy compared to static approaches, real-time 30fps processing at 480 $$\times $$ × 270 resolution, and up to 18 $$\times $$ × improvement in frame processing rates during closed-loop navigation tasks. These computational efficiency gains translate to substantial energy savings, achieving 6.9W power reduction on NVIDIA Jetson TX2 hardware through proportional decreases in processing time and computational load.
